Welcome toA Star in a Gas Cloud

A hot star floods a hydrogen cloud with ionising light: how far does its glow reach?

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

About: the Strömgren sphere: counting the star's ionising photons against the recombinations in the gas fixes the size of an H II region

About this simulation

On screen
Left: the star and its cloud on the sky, on fixed axes from −8 to 8 pc at equal scales. The neutral hydrogen is a dim grey haze everywhere; the ionised gas is a pale red Hα disc of radius rS with a sharp edge and an arrow rS from the star to that edge. Violet streaks are ionising photons, each stopping inside the disc where it ionises an atom; red flashes are recombinations. A 1.30 pc bar shows the distance from the Sun to its nearest neighbouring star. Right: the neutral fraction against r from 0 to 8 pc, with a dashed line at 1 for fully neutral and a tick at rS.
Controls
The ionising photon rate Ṅion of the star, 1048 to 1050 per second, and the hydrogen density nH, 108 to 109 per cubic metre, both on logarithmic sliders; the chips under each slider set the exact values the questions use. The sphere takes its steady-state size at once. The Readouts panel in the sidebar lists the radius, the total recombinations per second and, at the end, the thickness of the edge.
Measured
rS = (3Ṅion / 4π nH² αrec)1/3 with αrec = 2.6 × 10−19 m³/s, in parsecs and light-years; the total recombinations per second are (4π/3) rS³ nH² αrec. Photons and flashes are drawn at 30 per second for every 1049 photons per second the star emits; the photons cross the sphere in about a second, light slowed down enormously.
Assumptions
Pure hydrogen at one uniform density, in a steady state. That state is reached after about one recombination time, 1/(nHαrec) ≈ 1200 years at 108 m−3. The ionised gas is at about 104 K, where αrec = 2.6 × 10−19 m³/s; recombinations straight to the ground state are left out, because the photon each one emits is absorbed again close by (case B). There is no dust and the sphere does not move: real H II regions then expand, since the hot ionised gas is overpressured. The edge thickness is the mean free path 1/(nHσ) in neutral gas with σ = 6 × 10−22 m², the cross-section at the ionisation threshold.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Neutral fraction with distance

Set the ionising photon rate to 1049 s−1 and the hydrogen density to 108 m−3. Before looking at the inset, predict how the fraction of the hydrogen that is neutral changes as you go out from the star.

2 · A brighter star

Keep the hydrogen density at 108 m−3 and the photon rate at 1049 s−1. Before raising the photon rate to 8 × 1049 s−1, eight times as many photons per second, predict what happens to the radius of the sphere.

3 · Denser gas

Set the photon rate back to 1049 s−1. Before raising the hydrogen density from 108 to 8 × 108 m−3, predict what happens to the radius of the sphere.

4 · Counting the recombinations

Keep the settings of question 3. A Recombinations readout appears once you answer. Before it does, predict how the total number of recombinations per second in the whole sphere, and the rate of red flashes, compare with the sphere of question 1.

5 · The edge of a big sphere

Set the photon rate to 1050 s−1 and the hydrogen density to 108 m−3, the largest sphere the controls allow. Before looking at the inset, predict what the edge of this larger sphere looks like.

6 · Summary

A hot star keeps the gas around it ionised out to the Strömgren radius rS, where its ionising photons are all used up re-ionising atoms that recombine: photons out of the star = recombinations in the sphere.

Ṅion = (4π/3) rS3 nH2 αrec, so rS ∝ Ṅion1/3 nH−2/3. The edge is sharp, about one photon mean free path thick (now in the Readouts).

Real H II regions do not stay this size: the ionised gas at about 104 K is at far higher pressure than the cold gas around it, so the sphere then expands.

A Hot Star in a Hydrogen Cloud

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A hot star in a cloud of hydrogen gas ionises the gas around it. This sim sets the star's ionising photon rate and the gas density, and shows the region that results and how neutral the gas is at each distance.

What you'll learn

  • How the photon rate and the gas density set the size of the ionised region.
  • What keeps that region at its size while atoms keep recombining.
  • What the boundary between ionised and neutral gas is like.
  • How large the region is next to the spacing of the stars.
The sim's layout, drawn schematically: the cloud on the left, the inset axes on the right.

What's on screen

  • The ionised gas, the glowing disc, with a white arrow marking its radius rS.
  • Photons, violet dashes streaming out from the star, 30 per second for each 1049 s-1.
  • Red flashes, the recombinations, in the same proportion.
  • Scale bar, 1.3 pc, the distance from the Sun to the nearest star.
  • Inset on the right: the neutral fraction against distance r, with a dashed amber line at fully neutral.
See itWatch the opening cloud. Watch for: violet photons leaving the star and red flashes inside the glowing disc.

Fixed in the sim: a cloud of pure hydrogen at one uniform density, a recombination coefficient α = 2.6 × 10-19 m3 s-1 (the value at 104 K) and a photoionisation cross-section σ = 6 × 10-22 m2. The sim draws the finished region at once; it does not show it growing.

03

Ionisation balance fixes the radius of the ionised sphere

A photon with enough energy ionises a hydrogen atom, and an electron that later meets a proton recombines. In a uniform cloud of pure hydrogen the notes (eq. 6.11) count the recombinations in each cubic metre per second with the recombination coefficient α:

Inside the ionised region the gas is almost fully ionised, so ne = np = nH.

Once the region has settled, every photon the star emits is spent on one recombination. For a sphere of radius rS, of volume 4πrS³/3 (notes eq. 6.12):

The first line is the balance, the second its solution. The notes call rS the Strömgren radius.

At the opening values, Ṅion = 1049 s-1 and nH = 108 m-3, this gives rS = 3.150 pc, which is 10.27 ly.

The balance: photons emitted each second equal recombinations in the whole sphere each second.
Key idea. In the steady state the recombinations in the whole sphere each second equal the photons the star emits each second, and that fixes one radius.
See itLook at the opening readouts. Watch for: Recombinations reading 1.0×10⁴⁹ s⁻¹, the same as the photon rate, with rS = 3.150 pc.
04

The radius grows as the cube root of the photon rate and falls as the density to the power minus two thirds

The volume grows as rS³ and each cubic metre recombines at a rate proportional to nH², so the solution of the balance has two exponents. The radius rises as Ṅion to the power 1/3. Eight times the photons gives 81/3 = 2 times the radius, and ten times the photons gives only 101/3 = 2.15 times.

The radius falls as nH to the power −2/3. Eight times the density gives 8−2/3 = 1/4 of the radius, because denser gas recombines faster and a smaller volume already uses up the same photons. Ten times both gives 101/3 × 10−2/3 = 10−1/3 = 0.464.

Radius against photon rate for two densities. Both lines have the same slope, 1/3, on these logarithmic axes.
Ṅ nH

These sliders move the sim too. The radius and the recombinations come from the sim's own readouts.

Key idea. The radius is only the cube root of the photon rate, and the density works the other way, with a larger exponent.
See itRaise the photon rate from 10⁴⁹ to 8 × 10⁴⁹ s⁻¹. Watch for: rS going from 3.150 pc to 6.299 pc, exactly twice as large.
See itNow raise the density from 10⁸ to 8 × 10⁸ m⁻³. Watch for: rS falling from 3.150 pc to 0.787 pc, a quarter, while the recombinations stay at 10⁴⁹ s⁻¹.
05

The ionised region ends at a front about one photon mean free path thick

A photon in neutral hydrogen travels about one mean free path ℓ before an atom absorbs it (notes section 6.1):

The sim shows ℓ as the Edge thickness. At 108 m-3 it is 5.40 × 10-4 pc.

Inside rS almost every atom is ionised, so the photons cross the sphere freely. Near rS they have nearly all been used up, and the rest are absorbed within a few ℓ. The neutral fraction rises from nearly zero to one in that thin shell, the ionisation front, about 1.7 × 10-4 of rS at the opening values.

Neutral fraction against r. The zoom is a schematic: the true front is far narrower than one pixel, so the sim draws it as a step.

ℓ depends on the density alone. At 1050 s-1 the radius is 6.786 pc and ℓ is still 5.40 × 10-4 pc.

Key idea. The glow does not fade out. The photons are used up in a front about one mean free path thick, far thinner than the sphere.
See itSet the photon rate to 10⁵⁰ s⁻¹. Watch for: rS reading 6.786 pc, the edge thickness still 5.4×10⁻⁴ pc, and a step at rS in the inset.
06

The sphere is a few parsecs across, and the sim shows only the settled balance

The scale bar, 1.30 pc, is the Sun's distance to the nearest star. The opening sphere is 2.42 times that. At 1050 s-1 it is 5.22 times, and at 109 m-3 it is 0.679 pc, 0.52 times. Over both sliders rS runs from 0.315 pc to 6.786 pc.

The balance holds once the gas has settled. A proton waits about 1/(nH α) before it captures an electron: 3.8 × 1010 s, about 1200 years, at 108 m-3, much shorter than the lifetime of an O star (notes).

The sim leaves out dust, helium, varying density and any change after the balance. Its α counts only recombinations into excited levels, because a recombination into the ground level makes a photon that ionises an atom nearby. The photon rate depends steeply on the star's temperature: a star twice as hot emits over 100 times as many (notes problem 3).

Key idea. Over the sliders the sphere runs from a quarter of the Sun's distance to the nearest star to over five times it.
See itRaise the density from 10⁸ to 10⁹ m⁻³. Watch for: rS shrinking from 3.150 pc to 0.679 pc, and the edge thickness from 5.4×10⁻⁴ to 5.4×10⁻⁵ pc.
07

Summary

In one line. A hot star ionises the gas around it; the sim shows how the size of that ionised region depends on the star and on the cloud.

Common mix-ups

  • "Starlight thins as 1/r², so the neutral fraction fades in steadily." The photons are used up, so the neutral fraction stays near zero out to rS and rises in a front 5.4 × 10-4 pc thick.
  • "Eight times the photons gives a sphere eight times wider." The radius follows the cube root: 3.150 pc becomes 6.299 pc, twice as large.
  • "Denser gas means more atoms to ionise, so a bigger sphere." It recombines faster, and 8 times the density gives 0.787 pc, a quarter of the radius.
  • "A larger sphere has a blurrier edge." The front depends on the density only: at 1050 s-1 it is still 5.4 × 10-4 pc.

Things to try on your own

  • Raise both the photon rate and the density tenfold. The radius changes by 10-1/3 = 0.464, from 3.150 pc to 1.462 pc.
  • Set 1048 s-1 and 109 m-3 to find the smallest sphere, 0.315 pc.
